questions.q: What is the core idea of RAG?
options: Look up relevant text first and hand it to the model with the question, shrinking its job from 'know everything' to 'read this and answer'
questions.explain: LLMs are extremely good at reading provided text and answering.

questions.q: Which two problems does RAG solve?
questions.explain: A plain model can only refuse or guess about private or recent data.

questions.q: Why not paste the entire knowledge base into every prompt?
options: It doesn't fit, it costs too much on every request, and accuracy degrades with facts buried in the middle
questions.explain: A 1M-token window is roughly 3–4 MB; real collections are gigabytes.

questions.q: How does grounding change the hallucination failure profile?
options: The model can quote and cite real passages and be told to say 'I don't know' when the text lacks the answer
questions.explain: It doesn't make hallucination impossible.

questions.q: What property makes embeddings useful for retrieval?
options: Texts that mean similar things get close vectors, even with no words in common
questions.explain: 'How do I get my money back?' lands near 'refund policy'.

questions.q: What does a cosine similarity near 0 mean?
questions.explain: 1.0 is the same direction; −1.0 is opposite (rare).

questions.q: What is the vector shape of all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings?
questions.explain: Each text becomes a point in a 384-dimensional space.

questions.q: Why does semantic search beat keyword search for 'money back' vs 'refund'?
options: Keyword search can't match words with no overlap, while embeddings capture meaning
questions.explain: The individual numbers are meaningless; relative position matters.

questions.q: Why does chunking matter so much?
options: Retrieval returns chunks, the LLM reads chunks and evaluation scores chunks, so wrong chunks can't be fixed downstream
questions.explain: It's the least glamorous and most consequential decision.

questions.q: What two forces pull chunk size in opposite directions?
options: Embedding models truncate long input, while the LLM needs enough context in each chunk
questions.explain: Chunks must be small enough for one coherent topic and large enough to be useful evidence.

questions.q: Why use overlap in fixed-size chunking?
options: A fixed slicer will cut ideas in half; overlap ensures at least one chunk holds the whole thought
questions.explain: Typical overlap is 10–20%, at the cost of near-duplicate chunks.

questions.q: For 2000 'A' characters with chunk_size 800 and overlap 150, what are the chunk lengths?
questions.explain: The start advances by chunk_size − overlap = 650: chunks begin at 0, 650, 1300 and 1950, so the lengths are 800, 800, 700 and 50. (The lesson's printed output shows 800 for the third chunk, which is a typo.)

questions.q: What are a vector database's four jobs?
questions.explain: Records are (id, vector, text, metadata).

questions.q: Why index vectors with ANN structures such as HNSW?
options: To find nearest neighbors without comparing against every vector, with near-perfect results in a fraction of the time
questions.explain: It's approximate nearest-neighbor search.

questions.q: What does metadata filtering add?
options: Restricting search to records whose metadata matches, such as source == 'policy.md', which pure vector math can't do
questions.explain: Filtering complements similarity.

questions.q: What is the same-model rule for a collection?
options: One collection per corpus per embedding model; queries must use the same model that embedded the documents
questions.explain: Mixing models breaks similarity.

questions.q: What does the shared retrieve(question, k, where) function return?
options: The top-k nearest chunks, optionally restricted by metadata
questions.explain: This exact shape appears in every RAG system.

questions.q: What does a similarity threshold (MAX_DISTANCE) do?
options: Drops weak matches so the system can say it doesn't know instead of using irrelevant chunks
questions.explain: It's a retrieval confidence threshold.

questions.q: Why does retrieval matter more than anything after it?
options: Generation can only be as good as the chunks it receives
questions.explain: Everything after retrieval depends on what it returns.

questions.q: What does metadata filtering let you do in a knowledge base?
options: Search only a source or topic, e.g. topic == 'refunds'
questions.explain: The corpus tags each chunk with source and topic.

questions.q: Why tag each context chunk with a number and source?
options: The tags make citations like [1] possible
They are required by the API
questions.explain: build_context formats '[i] (source: ...)'.

questions.q: Why does the prompt say to use ONLY the provided context?
options: It's the grounding instruction separating RAG from the model freestyling; otherwise it blends retrieved facts with guesses
questions.explain: Without it you can't tell facts from guesses.

questions.q: What should the model do if the context lacks the answer?
options: Say exactly 'I don't know based on the available documents.' and not guess
questions.explain: An honest don't-know path is part of the design.

questions.q: Which piece is the only paid/networked part of the pipeline?
options: The generation call to the Anthropic API
questions.explain: The pattern is the same for any chat-completions API.

questions.q: What stages does the minimal rag.py pipeline contain?
options: Ingest → chunk → embed → store → retrieve → generate
questions.explain: It's about 100 lines with no framework.

questions.q: What does the persistent ChromaDB path give you?
options: The index survives between runs, so you ingest once and ask many times
questions.explain: The script has 'ingest' and 'ask' commands.

questions.q: How does chunk_text pack content?
options: Paragraphs (falling back to sentences) into chunks of at most max_chars
questions.explain: It avoids cutting mid-idea.

questions.q: What is the pipeline the skeleton for?
questions.explain: The capstone grows from it.

questions.q: Why is RAG evaluation hard?
options: Two coupled stages (retrieval and generation), no single right answer, and small samples mislead
questions.explain: Measure the stages separately.

questions.q: What is in a golden question set?
options: Questions with expected answers and known relevant chunk ids, including deliberate unanswerable questions
questions.explain: A pipeline that never says 'I don't know' fails the unanswerable ones.

questions.q: Why include unanswerable questions on purpose?
options: To catch pipelines that never admit they don't know
questions.explain: Those expected answers are 'I don't know based on the available documents.'

questions.q: How many questions should you start with?
options: 20+, growing over time as users hit failures
questions.explain: With 5 questions one flake swings your score by 20 points.

questions.q: How do you confirm a bad-chunking failure?
options: Print the retrieved chunks; if boundaries sever sentences, tables or Q→A pairs, that's it
questions.explain: Fix with structure-aware chunking, more overlap and one topic per chunk.

questions.q: Why do embeddings miss exact identifiers like ERR_4012 or part numbers?
options: Embeddings treat exact tokens as noise; add keyword/BM25 search alongside dense retrieval (hybrid)
questions.explain: Hybrid search exists because embeddings whiff on exact tokens.

questions.q: A user says 'can't log in' but docs say 'authentication failure'. What kind of retrieval miss is this?
options: A vocabulary mismatch the embedding model can't bridge
questions.explain: Check whether the right chunk is at rank 7 (ranking) or rank 400 (vocabulary).

questions.q: What does context overflow look like?
options: API errors about maximum context length, or costs and latency creeping up as k is raised
questions.explain: Top-k chunks, scaffolding and history exceed the window or waste money.

questions.q: What does the capstone Docs Q&A bot do?
options: Ingests docs, answers in a CLI loop with cited sources, refuses ungrounded questions, and ships a golden-set eval
questions.explain: It's a tiny multi-file project.

questions.q: Why put every tunable in config.py?
options: Evaluation tells you how to set them, and they live in one place
questions.explain: For example CHUNK_MAX_CHARS, TOP_K and MAX_DISTANCE.

questions.q: What does MAX_DISTANCE = 0.8 do in the bot?
options: Drops hits above that cosine distance so weak matches aren't used
questions.explain: It supports the honest don't-know path.

questions.q: What does evaluate.py measure?
options: Hit rate, MRR and an LLM-judge score on the golden set
questions.explain: It lets you keep proving it works as you change things.

questions.q: What blind spot do embeddings have that BM25 covers?
options: Exact tokens such as error codes, order ids and rare product names
questions.explain: A vector store returns something semantically adjacent but wrong.

questions.q: Which three ideas does BM25 formalize?
options: Term frequency (diminishing returns), inverse document frequency (rare terms matter more) and length normalization
questions.explain: A term in a 10-word doc is stronger evidence than in a 1000-word doc.

questions.q: Why does matching 'E4022' tell you more than matching 'the'?
options: Rare words carry the signal (high IDF)
questions.explain: Common words appear everywhere.

questions.q: Why is sparse retrieval cheap?
options: It needs no embedding model, API key or GPU
questions.explain: The lesson ran everything with rank-bm25 and the standard library.

questions.q: Why run both dense and sparse retrieval?
options: They have opposite blind spots: BM25 misses 'undo a bad release' while embeddings find the rollback doc, and embeddings miss exact tokens
questions.explain: Hybrid search merges their results.

questions.q: Why can't you just add BM25 and dense scores?
options: They live on incompatible scales (BM25 up to ~7.5, cosine up to ~0.63)
questions.explain: Fusion needs a scale-free method such as rank-based merging.

questions.q: Why does the key design point make fusion a ten-line function?
options: Both retrievers expose the same interface: a query in, an ordered list of document indices out
questions.explain: No refactor needed.

questions.q: What was the 'dense' channel in that lesson's examples, honestly?
options: A character n-gram TF-IDF stand-in, still lexical, so it doesn't solve vocabulary mismatch
questions.explain: The lesson states what ran and what didn't.

questions.q: What is the two-stage pipeline in reranking?
options: Cast a wide, cheap net (e.g. 50 candidates), then re-score only the survivors with a cross-encoder
questions.explain: It routinely moves the right document from rank 7 to rank 1 without touching the index.

questions.q: How does a cross-encoder differ from a bi-encoder?
options: It feeds the query and document through the model together so every query token attends to every document token
questions.explain: A bi-encoder embeds the query and documents separately.

questions.q: Why can't you cross-encode a 100,000-document corpus at query time?
options: It needs a full forward pass per (query, document) pair, which is impossible at that scale
questions.explain: So retrieve about 50 first, then rerank those.

questions.q: What did the lesson say honestly about its reranker?
options: It used a pair-scoring stand-in; pipeline shape and rank movement are real but quality and cost numbers aren't representative
questions.explain: Real cross-encoders need torch and sentence-transformers.

questions.q: Why is the query often the weakest link?
options: Users type short, typo'd or context-dependent queries while documents are careful formal prose, a translation problem
questions.explain: Rewriting turns a bad query into one or more good ones.

questions.q: What is multi-query retrieval?
options: Send queries in parallel to different users
Generate several phrasings and fuse their rankings (e.g. with RRF)
questions.explain: The variants were hard-coded in the lesson; production uses an LLM.

questions.q: Why does the rank function filter s[i] > 0?
options: A 0.0 score is not a hit; otherwise it returns corpus-order documents that fusion can't distinguish from real hits
questions.explain: All-zero rankings poison the fusion.

questions.q: What does an empty BM25 result for 'undo a bad release' show?
options: The query shares no vocabulary with the rollback runbook
questions.explain: The answer exists; the words don't overlap.

questions.q: Why does semantic similarity not replace metadata filters?
options: It can't express hard constraints like 'only documents this user may see' or 'only the current policy version'
questions.explain: These are correctness and security boundaries.

questions.q: Why capture metadata at ingestion time?
options: Metadata you didn't capture doesn't exist; re-indexing to add a field is expensive and sometimes impossible
questions.explain: Ask what someone will want to filter on in six months.

questions.q: Why store dates as numbers rather than strings?
options: Numbers support $gte and ordering; strings only support equality and mislead about ordering
questions.explain: year: 2025 supports range filters.

questions.q: Why capture security fields like tenant_id on day one?
options: Retrofitting after launch is a migration and an incident report
questions.explain: In multi-tenant systems metadata is a security boundary.

questions.q: Why do tables break prose-style RAG?
options: A cell like 99 is meaningless without its column header and row label, and chunking scatters that context
questions.explain: Chunks that each look fine say nothing.

questions.q: Why can't retrieval answer 'how many seats total?'
options: Those are aggregations; retrieval cannot sum, so no top-k tuning computes SUM(seats)
questions.explain: Use text-to-SQL or code for aggregation.

questions.q: What is row-level verbalization?
options: Turn each row into a self-contained sentence that carries its own headers
questions.explain: Strategy B in the lesson.

questions.q: What is the problem with the whole table as one chunk?
options: It is too small to embed
Every row retrieves together, the LLM may read the wrong row, and it doesn't scale to large tables
questions.explain: For example Enterprise's SLA pulled onto the Team plan.

questions.q: Why is ingestion where most RAG quality is won or lost?
options: A retriever can't outperform its input; repeated boilerplate pollutes BM25 statistics and drags embeddings together
questions.explain: Every chunk inheriting a header becomes a high-frequency term.

questions.q: What does a PDF actually contain?
options: Instructions for drawing glyphs at coordinates, so reading order and headings are reconstructed heuristically
questions.explain: The parser may get it wrong.

questions.q: How does the lesson detect boilerplate without hard-coding it?
options: Text that repeats across pages (plus patterns like 'Page N of M') is boilerplate
questions.explain: You don't need to know what it says.

questions.q: What was not executed in this lesson?
options: The .docx section (described in prose) and OCR
questions.explain: python-docx wasn't installed for the run.

questions.q: What is LangChain's genuine value for RAG?
options: Composition: many loaders, splitters, store adapters and retrievers sharing an interface, so swapping a store or adding a reranker is a one-line change
questions.explain: It wraps what you already built by hand.

questions.q: Which LangChain abstraction corresponds to your own rrf() fusion?
questions.explain: ContextualCompressionRetriever wraps a cross-encoder reranker.

questions.q: Why does the lesson warn that none of its code was executed?
options: The packages weren't installed, so there are no verified outputs; treat it as a map of the API surface
questions.explain: Check the version's docs before copying.

questions.q: Why learn the pieces by hand before using a framework?
options: Frameworks are easier to evaluate, and harder to be fooled by, when you know what they wrap
questions.explain: The mapping table is the curriculum.

questions.q: How does LlamaIndex differ from LangChain?
options: It is a general agent framework
It is built specifically for connecting LLMs to data, with Index and QueryEngine abstractions and opinions about retrieval
questions.explain: LangChain gives you a Retriever to compose.

questions.q: Why is the three-line LlamaIndex version dangerous?
options: It silently chooses chunk size, embedding model, top_k, prompt and LLM, every knob you should tune
questions.explain: Use it to check data loads, not to decide whether RAG works for your problem.

questions.q: What is a LlamaIndex Node?
options: A chunk plus relationships to its neighbours
questions.explain: A Document is the source file with metadata.

questions.q: What does a QueryEngine represent?
questions.explain: It maps to your own answer function.

questions.q: What is the skill this project builds?
options: Proving which techniques earn their keep on your corpus, and deleting those that don't
questions.explain: In the reference run, two of four configurations bought nothing.

questions.q: Why does config.py give every technique a feature flag?
options: You cannot ablate what you cannot switch off
questions.explain: Each flag is a row in the ablation table.

questions.q: Which five techniques does the project test?
options: BM25, hybrid fusion, reranking, query expansion and metadata filtering
questions.explain: Each costs latency, complexity or money.

questions.q: How should you read the reference numbers?
options: They're real numbers from real code but not a claim about production corpora with real embeddings; produce your own table
questions.explain: The dense channel was a TF-IDF stand-in.

questions.q: What makes RAG 'agentic'?
options: Retrieval becomes a tool the model can call zero or more times in a loop it steers, deciding whether evidence is enough or to rephrase
questions.explain: The LLM controls retrieval decisions instead of your pipeline code.

questions.q: Why does the loop have a Budget capping tool calls?
options: To stop runaway loops and cost; exceeding it raises an error
questions.explain: It's the trap the lesson warns about.

questions.q: What question shapes break single-shot RAG?
options: Ones needing judgment about retrieval itself: is the evidence enough, should I rephrase, do I need a second different search
questions.explain: One search can't cover the other half of the question.

questions.q: Why does the lesson hardcode the model's subqueries?
options: So the control flow is inspectable; a real agent generates them
questions.explain: A real system hands the LLM a search tool schema.

questions.q: Why does single-shot retrieval fail on 'Who acquired the company where Acme's founder used to work?'
options: No chunk holds the whole answer; the facts are in separate chunks that don't share the query's words
questions.explain: Only the founder chunk overlaps with the query.

questions.q: What is the decompose-then-chain approach?
options: Break the question into ordered sub-questions and feed each hop's evidence into the next query
questions.explain: It lets hop 2 find 'Globex' even though the sub-question doesn't name it.

questions.q: How many hops does the example need?
questions.explain: Jane Rivera → Globex → Initech.

questions.q: Who acquired Globex in the corpus?
questions.explain: The chain ends at chunk 3.

questions.q: What does GraphRAG retrieve by?
options: Traversal of an explicit entity-relation graph instead of text similarity
questions.explain: It answers 'how are these entities connected?'

questions.q: Why does a vector retriever fail to surface Initech for the query 'Jane Rivera'?
options: Nothing about Initech is semantically close to her name; the connection is structural
questions.explain: Two hops in the graph reach Initech.

questions.q: What do community summaries add in Microsoft-style GraphRAG?
options: The graph is clustered into communities and pre-summarized, so a query can retrieve one dense summary instead of walking edges
questions.explain: It avoids edge walks at query time.

questions.q: What is networkx standing in for?
options: A graph store such as Neo4j in production
questions.explain: The traversal logic is the same.

questions.q: What are the two index families underneath production vector databases?
options: HNSW (multi-layer neighbor graph) and IVF (clustered buckets)
questions.explain: HNSW has logarithmic query time; IVF is cheaper to build/update at some recall cost.

questions.q: How much memory do 10M float32 vectors of 768 dimensions need as a flat index?
Which databases does the lesson compare?
questions.explain: Chroma is local, single-process and embedded.

questions.q: Why was this lesson manual review rather than runnable code?
options: No local service for these databases was available in the sandbox; the memory math is real arithmetic
questions.explain: The lesson says so plainly.

questions.q: Why does MTEB leaderboard rank matter least for your corpus?
options: It's an average over 56 datasets in domains none of which is yours, so a top model can underperform on your tickets, contracts or code
questions.explain: Benchmark on your own data.

questions.q: How do you benchmark an embedding model on your data?
options: Make an eval set of (query, answering doc) pairs and measure top-1 (or recall@k) accuracy
questions.explain: The lesson's TF-IDF baseline scored 1/3.

questions.q: Why did TF-IDF score only 0.33 on the eval set?
options: It's lexical: 'refund' and 'money-back' don't overlap, and shared words like 'api' mislead
questions.explain: It's bad in a very informative way for this lesson.

questions.q: What does the lesson weigh besides accuracy?
options: The dimension/cost trade-off and when fine-tuning beats picking another off-the-shelf model
questions.explain: Higher dimensions cost more storage and compute.

questions.q: What does context precision measure?
options: Of what was relevant, how much you retrieved
Of what you retrieved, how much was relevant
questions.explain: Recall is the reverse.

questions.q: retrieved = [0, 3, 4] and relevant = {0, 3}. What are precision and recall?
questions.explain: Two of three retrieved are relevant; both relevant docs were found.

questions.q: Why track precision alongside recall?
options: A pipeline can hit 100% recall by over-retrieving
questions.explain: Full recall with 67% precision is a normal pair of scores.

questions.q: What does faithfulness measure?
options: Of the answer's claims, how many are supported by the context
questions.explain: It catches hallucination.

questions.q: Which step dominates a synchronous RAG request's latency?
questions.explain: Steps 1–3 are usually 50–300ms combined.

questions.q: Which lever targets which step?
options: Streaming targets generation; caching targets embedding/search/rerank; parallelism targets sharded vector search
questions.explain: Each attacks a different part of the budget.

questions.q: Why does a production cache key on normalized or similarity matches?
options: Near-duplicate queries like 'what's your refund policy' vs 'what is the refund policy' would miss an exact-hash cache
questions.explain: The lesson's exact-hash cache missed them.

questions.q: What did caching achieve in the measured example?
options: 5 calls dropped from 57.7 ms to 10.2 ms, more than 5x faster
questions.explain: One miss and four hits.

questions.q: What does content hashing tell you?
options: Which documents actually changed, so unchanged ones skip re-embedding, without trusting source timestamps
questions.explain: Timestamps are frequently wrong or absent.

questions.q: What does upsert return for identical content re-synced?
questions.explain: Different content returns 'reindexed' with version + 1.

questions.q: What is 'the part teams forget' in incremental indexing?
options: Deletes: otherwise a deleted refund policy keeps being retrieved forever
questions.explain: Reconcile against the authoritative source set.

questions.q: Why isn't re-embedding the whole corpus on every change acceptable?
options: A one-line edit shouldn't cost a million embedding calls
questions.explain: It doesn't scale.

questions.q: Why record spans per stage rather than one log line per request?
options: Structured per-stage records answer 'what happened' without guessing which of five stages failed
questions.explain: You can query fields like retrieve.top_k scores.

questions.q: What does a Span hold?
options: A name, start and end time and arbitrary attributes
questions.explain: It's the unit used by OpenTelemetry, LangSmith and Phoenix.

questions.q: In the example, which stage dominated latency?
questions.explain: Tracing shows which stage dominates and what the retrieval scores were.

questions.q: What does the module add besides tracing?
questions.explain: It also helps debug reports that 'the answer was wrong'.

questions.q: Which four modules does the agentic research assistant combine?
options: Agentic tool-calling with a budget, multi-hop decomposition, a query cache and a trace log per stage
questions.explain: It answers multi-fact questions within a call budget.

questions.q: Why does extract_entity take the last capitalized token?
options: A chunk mentions the already-known entity first, then the new one the next hop needs
questions.explain: Jane Rivera comes before Globex in the chunk.

questions.q: What does the cache avoid?
questions.explain: cached_search returns a hit flag.

questions.q: What does the trace leave behind?
options: An inspectable record of every decision
questions.explain: It supports debugging.

questions.q: What is the risk of a single shared index with per-tenant metadata filters?
options: A missing or wrong filter leaks data across tenants
questions.explain: It is the cheapest to operate and the riskiest.

questions.q: What does index-per-tenant guarantee?
options: Structural isolation: no code path touches two tenants' data, at the cost of N indexes to run
questions.explain: Small tenants pay disproportionate fixed overhead.

questions.q: Why do enterprises grow into hub-and-spoke?
options: A central retrieval service handles auth, routing, observability and policies once, scaling the platform team's effort sub-linearly
questions.explain: Teams own their data and ingestion.

questions.q: Why is much of this module deliberately manual review?
options: 'Which architecture fits your org' can't be validated by a toy script
questions.explain: Runnable code appears only for genuinely code-level decisions.

questions.q: What is the vulnerable pattern?
options: Filter after ranking: rank across all tenants, then discard non-matches
questions.explain: The order of two operations is the whole security model.

questions.q: What happens in the lesson when tenant acme queries Globex's wording with a post-filter?
options: It returns [] (denies acme their own data) because the top global hit belonged to Globex
questions.explain: A post-filter can deny a tenant their own data or leak another's.

questions.q: What does the safe pre-filter do?
options: Restrict candidates to the tenant's documents first, then rank only within them
questions.explain: It returned acme's Q3 revenue.

questions.q: Why is this bug a data breach rather than a performance detail?
options: Under the right query the system can hand a tenant someone else's data
questions.explain: Isolation must be enforced before ranking.

questions.q: In the cost model, where does almost all the money go?
options: The LLM call: prompt input and generated output tokens (embedding cost was $0.40 of $8,310)
questions.explain: Teams instinctively optimize embeddings and retrieval speed, but the money is in generation.

questions.q: For 1M queries, ~1,520 input tokens and 250 output tokens each, what is the approximate total?
questions.explain: LLM input $4,560 plus output $3,750 plus tiny embedding cost.

questions.q: What does a 30% cache hit rate save in the example?
questions.explain: Cached queries skip a fresh LLM call.

questions.q: If the goal is specifically cost, where should you look first?
options: The LLM call: context tokens and output length
questions.explain: Retrieval optimization still matters for latency and quality.

questions.q: Why did parallelizing three retrieval shards save only 78 ms?
options: Generation (1800 ms) dwarfs everything else; optimize the stage that dominates, not the easiest to parallelize
questions.explain: Sequential 1963 ms vs parallel 1885 ms.

questions.q: What does a 1% straggler on one of three shards do to p99?
options: It turns p99 into about 7x p50 (46.8 ms vs 331.3 ms)
questions.explain: Parallel retrieval waits for the slowest shard.

questions.q: Why is p99, not the average, the number that matters?
options: Averages hide the slow requests that generate a steady stream of complaints
questions.explain: Fast on average still has slow-request complaints.

questions.q: How can you reduce perceived latency even if total time doesn't change?
questions.explain: Streaming makes the first words appear quickly.

questions.q: What is indirect prompt injection in RAG?
options: A user typing a bad prompt
A malicious instruction planted in a document that later gets retrieved into the LLM's context, where the model may follow it
questions.explain: The attack doesn't need to come from the user's message.

questions.q: Why do RAG systems have a larger attack surface than a plain chatbot?
options: Any ingestion source (tickets, scraped pages, uploads, emails) is a potential injection vector
questions.explain: Ingestion pipelines are built for correctness and freshness, not adversarial content.

questions.q: What is the security model for retrieved context?
questions.explain: Treat it that way throughout.

questions.q: What is a first line of defense shown in the lesson?
options: Pattern-based flagging of phrases like 'ignore previous instructions' or 'api key'
questions.explain: It is only a first line, not a complete defense.

questions.q: What must enterprise RAG answer in an audit?
options: Who asked what, what data informed the answer, who could have seen it, and how long the record is kept
questions.explain: 'It worked in testing' isn't a defense.

questions.q: Why log query, retrieval and generation as separate entries?
options: Each is independently attributable, so an auditor can see which document informed which answer
questions.explain: A single combined line loses that detail.

questions.q: What does the entry hash provide?
options: A cheap way to detect that an entry was altered after the fact (not a secure chain by itself)
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit about its limits.

questions.q: What is data lineage?
options: Mapping an answer back to the source documents and their metadata that informed it
questions.explain: For example source, classification and ingestion date.

questions.q: What does continuous evaluation catch that a CI regression suite doesn't?
options: Quality drift from a shifting corpus or user population, or a provider silently updating a model, none of which show up as a code diff
questions.explain: It uses production-traffic evaluation and feedback loops.

questions.q: In the example, thumbs-up rates were 0.86, 0.845 and 0.65 across three weeks. Which drop is real?
options: Week 3's drop to 0.65, an injected regression; the week 1 vs 2 gap is sampling noise
questions.explain: A 10-point threshold stays quiet on noise and fires on the real drop.

questions.q: What happens if the regression threshold is too tight or too loose?
options: Too tight false-alarms on normal variance; too loose lets real regressions slip through for weeks
questions.explain: The right threshold depends on feedback volume.

questions.q: How does higher traffic volume help?
options: It lets you tighten the threshold and catch smaller regressions faster
questions.explain: This is a statistics problem as much as an engineering one.

questions.q: What does RAG change versus fine-tuning?
options: RAG changes what the model knows right now by handing it facts at query time; fine-tuning changes what it does by default (tone, format, behavior)
questions.explain: RAG never changes weights.

questions.q: What happens if you fine-tune a model to know current pricing?
options: It's wrong the moment pricing changes, since facts are baked into weights needing a whole new training run
questions.explain: Use RAG for facts that change.

questions.q: What happens if you use RAG to make a model sound like your brand voice?
options: It doesn't, since retrieved documents give facts, not a persistent behavioral pattern
questions.explain: That's a job for fine-tuning.

questions.q: In the illustration, how much more does updating one fact cost via fine-tuning than via RAG?
options: About 12.5 million times, and hours instead of seconds
questions.explain: RAG: one embedding call for one chunk; fine-tune: a $50, 3-hour run.

questions.q: Which two levers dominate scaling ingestion?
questions.explain: They interact in ways worth measuring.

questions.q: Why was 10-way parallelism only 3.9x faster?
options: Thread-scheduling overhead, and past a point you're bound by the embedding provider's rate limit, risking 429s
questions.explain: I/O-bound calls overlap, but not perfectly.

questions.q: Why does batching help?
options: It amortizes the fixed per-request overhead that single-doc calls pay every time
questions.explain: Total time falls steeply as batch size grows.

questions.q: What is the risk of an ingestion pipeline that's too slow?
options: The index stays stale for hours
questions.explain: At millions of documents it can become the bottleneck.

questions.q: Which four pieces does the capstone combine?
options: Tenant-scoped retrieval, a tenant-scoped cache, injection detection on retrieved content and an audit log
questions.explain: It enforces isolation with a real assertion.

questions.q: How does tenant_scoped_search stay safe?
options: It filters to the tenant's documents before ranking
questions.explain: That's module 2's safe pattern.

questions.q: Why is the cache tenant-scoped?
options: A shared cache could return one tenant's cached answer to another
questions.explain: The cache key includes the tenant.

questions.q: What does the audit log capture?
options: Every query, retrieval and security event
questions.explain: It supports compliance review.

questions.q:
What does this print?
```
def chunk_fixed(text, size=800, overlap=150):
    out=[]; start=0
    while start < len(text):
        out.append(text[start:start+size]); start += size-overlap
    return out
print([len(c) for c in chunk_fixed('A'*2000)])
```
questions.explain: Starts advance by 650: chunks begin at 0, 650, 1300 and 1950, with lengths 800, 800, 700 and 50.
Two of three retrieved are relevant; both relevant docs were retrieved.
a and b tie on the fused score; sorted() is stable so a stays first, then c beats d.

questions.q:
What does this print?
```
import hashlib
h=lambda t: hashlib.sha256(t.encode()).hexdigest()
print(h('Refunds within 30 days.')==h('Refunds within 30 days.'), h('30 days')==h('45 days'))
```
questions.explain: Content hashing detects whether a document changed, so unchanged ones skip re-embedding.

questions.q:
What does this print?
```
docs=[('acme','a rev $2M'),('globex','g rev $5M')]
q={'g','rev'}
post=[d for d in sorted(docs,key=lambda d:-len(q&set(d[1].split())))[:1] if d[0]=='acme']
pre=sorted([d for d in docs if d[0]=='acme'],key=lambda d:-len(q&set(d[1].split())))[:1]
print(post, pre)
```
questions.explain: Filtering after ranking loses the tenant's own data when another tenant ranks first; filter before ranking.

questions.q: Users type 'card got rejected' but docs say 'payment declined'. What helps most?
questions.explain: It's a vocabulary mismatch.

questions.q: Queries contain error codes like E4022 that embeddings mangle. What do you add?
options: BM25 keyword search fused with dense retrieval (hybrid)
questions.explain: Embeddings are poor at exact tokens.

questions.q: The right chunk is at rank 7 but the LLM sees only the top 3. What is the highest-leverage fix?
options: Retrieve ~50 then rerank with a cross-encoder
questions.explain: Reranking can move the right document from rank 7 to rank 1.

questions.q: A question needs facts chained across three documents. What pattern helps?
questions.explain: Each hop's evidence feeds the next query.

questions.q: You must answer 'how many seats total across plans?' from a table. What approach fits?
options: Text-to-SQL or code over structured data; retrieval can't aggregate
questions.explain: Aggregations need computation, not retrieval.

questions.q: You want to know if a technique earns its keep. What do you do?
options: Run an ablation on a golden set with a flag per technique
questions.explain: Delete techniques that don't help your corpus.

questions.q: Your RAG answers are fluent but cite nothing relevant. Which metric flags that?
options: Faithfulness (are claims supported by the context) plus context precision
questions.explain: Faithfulness catches unsupported claims.

questions.q: A recall of 100% with low precision tells you what?
options: You over-retrieve; noise is entering the context
questions.explain: Track precision alongside recall.

questions.q: A policy doc is updated nightly. How do you keep the index fresh cheaply?
options: Content hashing with upserts and deletes, re-embedding only changed documents
questions.explain: Don't forget deletes, or removed policies keep being retrieved.

questions.q: A customer-uploaded PDF contains 'IGNORE ALL PREVIOUS INSTRUCTIONS'. What is this?
options: Indirect prompt injection; treat retrieved context as untrusted input
questions.explain: Any ingestion source is an injection vector.

questions.q: A multi-tenant system filters results after ranking. What can go wrong?
options: It can deny a tenant their own data or leak another's; filter before ranking
questions.explain: The order of operations is the security model.

questions.q: Your facts change weekly but you want the model to answer in a fixed brand voice. What do you combine?
options: RAG for facts plus fine-tuning (or prompting) for voice
questions.explain: They're complementary, not competitors.

questions.q: At a million queries a month, where does most of the cost go?
questions.explain: Reduce context size, output length or use caching.

questions.q: Your mean latency is fine but users complain. What should you check?
options: p99 latency, since stragglers dominate the tail
questions.explain: A 1% straggler can make p99 7x p50.

challenges.title: Chunk with overlap
challenges.prompt: Write `chunk_fixed(text, size, overlap)` that slices text into `size`-character chunks, advancing by `size - overlap`, and print the chunk lengths for 'A' * 25 with size 10 and overlap 3.
challenges.starter:
def chunk_fixed(text, size, overlap):
    # your code here
    pass

print([len(c) for c in chunk_fixed("A" * 25, 10, 3)])
challenges.solution:
def chunk_fixed(text, size, overlap):
    out, start = [], 0
    while start < len(text):
        out.append(text[start:start + size])
        start += size - overlap
    return out

print([len(c) for c in chunk_fixed("A" * 25, 10, 3)])
challenges.explain: The start advances by 7 each time: chunks start at 0, 7, 14 and 21.
